title: Three Artists and Two Writers On Surrealist Painter Remedios Varo's Influence
description: Like the Argentinian writer Samanta Schweblin, the first time I found myself in front of a painting by the Spanish-Mexican artist Remedios Varo (1
body:
Like the Argentinian writer Samanta Schweblin, the first time I found myself in front of a painting by the Spanish-Mexican artist Remedios Varo (1908-1963), I was stunned. Who was this elegant owl-figure with dainty fingers and feet? What was animating the creaturely machine at her side with tentacle-like brushes as hands? And, would I ever be able to look away?
Feeling mesmerized and awe-struck by Varo’s Surrealist visions isn’t an uncommon position to find oneself in. A new release from Louisiana Channel interviews three artists and two writers—Schweblin being one—about Varo’s influence, particularly her precise approach to alchemy and visualizing the thin veil between the physical and spiritual world. Interspersing artworks and commentary creates an insightful tapestry of a singular artist and her enduring legacy. Watch “Remedios Varo: The Painter of Magic” below, and learn more about the artist previously on Colossal.

title: On Concrete Remnants of London's Aylesbury Estate, Harriet Mena Hill Preserves a Community
description: Built throughout the 1960s and ’70s, the Aylesbury Estate is an enormous public housing complex in South East London that at its peak, boasted 11,
body:
Built throughout the 1960s and ’70s, the Aylesbury Estate is an enormous public housing complex in South East London that at its peak, boasted 11,000 residents. Like other social projects of this kind, Aylesbury has struggled with violence and vandalism throughout its run, and in 2005, local officials decided to demolish the estate and rebuild in phases rather than rehabilitate the existing structures.
Living and working in South East London for nearly four decades, Harriet Mena Hill was familiar with the area, but it wasn’t until 2018 when she was commissioned to teach a summer program for young residents that she really engaged with the project. She made large portraits from wool, blending dyed roving to delineate windows, shape bowed electrical wires, and even mimic graffiti spray-painted on outdoor walls. 
“Soft Concrete Missenden, Aylesbury Estate” (2020), wool on felt, 88 x 118 centimeters
Forming the series Soft Concrete, the textile pieces cast a largely gray environment of stone and steel in soft fiber. The body of work, Hill says, was a “repositioning of how the estate is perceived. Historically, it has been widely portrayed in the media as violent and intimidating, as a place without hope.” 
In contrast, Soft Concrete “presents the estate as a place of living and community. From a distance, the portraits look like photographs or realistic paintings, but on closer inspection, the material reveals itself to be wool, hand blended for subtle colour mixing used to depict small active details of domestic life,” the artist adds.
Hill is broadly interested in the ways that communities and the objects they interact with can become vessels for shared memories, so when the estate began to be razed in 2020, she started to collect fragments of concrete from the construction site. “It was a direct response to the situation of residents who were required to stay at home as the demolition of adjoining blocks, the homes of their former neighbours, continued throughout lockdown, in spite of wider restrictions,” she tells Colossal.
Before its destruction, several tenants had advocated for renovations rather than demolition, hoping to preserve the community and homes they’d built. In an interview with the BBC in 2023, long-time resident Aysen Dennis lamented being forced to leave the estate after 30 years. Local administrators found her new housing in central London, but it wasn’t the same. “The council gave me everything I asked for. It’s on a high floor. There’s lots of light. I can see the park,” Dennis said. “But it’s not my home.”
Studio view. Photo by Jon Cardwell
Intimate in scale, Hill’s paintings glimpse hallways and pockets of windows that are similarly sliced from their larger contexts, the ragged edges of concrete framing the largely domestic spaces. Part of the ongoing series titled The Aylesbury Fragments, the scenes capture the run-down infrastructure of buildings left standing during the phased reconstruction process. 
Although regeneration began in 2013, it’s less than half complete, and Hill has completed more than 150 paintings to date. As demolition continues, she adds to her ever-changing collection of concrete remnants. “I live with the unpainted pieces for months, sometimes years, getting to know their shape before I begin working on them,” the artist says, noting that as long as there are buildings still under construction, she’ll continue painting these small tributes to the community once housed within their walls.
Hill has exhibitions slated for London and across the U.K. throughout 2027. Follow along on Instagram.

“Stacked Sill.” Photo by Kevin Dutton
“Waiting.” Photo by Kevin Dutton
“Soft Concrete on the Aylesbury.” Photo by Alison Romanczuk
“Cable Drift.” Photo by Kevin Dutton
Studio view. Photo by Jon Cardwell
“Sudden In A Shaft of Sunlight.” Photo by Kevin Dutton

title: A Tribute to Black Soho Inside a New York Art Fair
description:
Feature
                Historic archives are displayed alongside works by Emma Amos, David Hammons, Vivian Browne, and more in
body:
Feature
                Historic archives are displayed alongside works by Emma Amos, David Hammons, Vivian Browne, and more in a presentation at Independent 20th Century.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Installation view of Black Soho, a booth by RYAN LEE and Salon 94 at Independent 20th Century (photo Valentina Di Liscia/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            “Camille — Here are 10 new slides for the ARCHIVES.” In the winter of 1988, Emma Amos scribbled a note to her friend and fellow artist, Camille Billops, along with a gift: an addition to her quickly multiplying library at 491 Broadway in Manhattan. Billops and her husband, James Hatch, bought the loft in 1973, where they lived and stewarded a compendium of Black artistic history throughout their life together. It came to house periodicals, scripts, photographs, audiotaped interviews, and more. The number of artists immortalized surpassed one thousand.An assortment of ephemera from the Billops-Hatch Collection now accompanies Black Soho, an exciting booth at the Independent 20th Century fair co-produced by RYAN LEE and Salon 94 galleries and on view through Sunday, September 27. The archival materials are displayed alongside artworks by Amos and Billops, as well as by Vivian Browne, David Hammons, Ed Clark, Norman Lewis, Frederick J. Brown, and Jean-Michel Basquiat, all of whom lived in or spent considerable time shaping the eponymous neighborhood, south of Houston Street.Emma Amos, “Eva the Babysitter” (1973) (© Emma Amos; courtesy RYAN LEE Gallery, New York)In conceiving the collaborative exhibition, gallerist Jeff Lee told Hyperallergic, they took inspiration from Billops and Hatch’s community-minded endeavors. “We wanted to emulate the energy of that loft. It was an incredible gathering space for so many major artists of her generation, but also younger generations,” said Lee.Black Soho is on view through the run of the fair. (photo Jasmine Weber/Hyperallergic)

title: No One Is Reading, Except at the New York Art Book Fair
description:
Feature
                The overlooked, subversive, and playful currents of politics and queer culture flow freely at the fair’s
body:
Feature
                The overlooked, subversive, and playful currents of politics and queer culture flow freely at the fair’s 20th anniversary edition, held at MoMA PS1. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Ruiqi Ma and Nathan Nam of com,,,as at the Printed Matter art book fair (all photos Lakshmi Rivera Amin/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            If Reading Rainbow’s opening sequence — the Y2K-techno-optimistic Chaka Khan version, to be exact — were a real place, it would be the outdoor zine tent at the New York Art Book Fair. I delight in never quite knowing what to expect from the annual gathering organized by Printed Matter, and this year was no different: Over 300 exhibitors from across the world come together at MoMA PS1 in Queens to form a giant, chimeric bookstore of sorts that feels unmistakably alive.On opening night of the fair’s 20th anniversary edition, which runs through the weekend, staffers handed us plastic string-closure folders, complete with lenticular Tweety Bird prints, for storing the many zines, flyers, and uncategorizable artworks we’d encounter inside. Across from artist Precious Okoyomon’s sculpture in the courtyard, the zine tent felt like a pocket-sized universe where marginalia is the text, and the overlooked, subversive, and playful currents of politics and queer culture flow freely.Staffers outside the fair handed us plastic string-closure folders to hold the treasures we'd encounter inside.Exhibit A: Art workers Jenna Hamed, Aya Krisht, and Rhonda Khalifeh of the Book Arts Solidarity Network handed out flyers for a publishers' meet-up after the fair, a space for connection beyond the museum’s walls. The organization first formed as a way to challenge book institutions’ silence on the genocide in Palestine, and is now launching its third annual edition of the MAKEREADY publication. For the risograph-printed booklet, they collected paintings, photographs, and written reflections from four artists in Gaza and South Lebanon, soon realizing that one thread connected all the works: the color yellow. Hamed explained that the process of assembling the poetic publication was “cathartic,” a way to process an era of bald imperialism and dispossession by centering the artists who are witnessing it.“It really came out of skill,” Hamed said of the organization’s ability to collaborate across borders. “We know what we’re doing.”

title: Here’s What (Dealers Said) Sold at the Armory Show
description:
Art Fairs
                If collectors had any concerns about the wars or inflation, they did not seem to share them at the New
body:
Art Fairs
                If collectors had any concerns about the wars or inflation, they did not seem to share them at the New York fair, where the mood was almost too serene.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Catinca Tabacaru exhibited in New York for the first time since leaving the Lower East Side in 2020. She stands next to Youssra Raouchi's “Fever Dream” (2025). (all photos Aaron Short/Hyperallergic unless noted)
    
        
            This week, the world outside the Armory Show has been embroiled in turmoil.Oil and food prices are soaring while mortgage rates topped 7%, which could compel the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates again next month. President Trump and other world leaders traded barbs at the United Nations over the Iran War as a resolution to call for the end of the conflict failed in the Senate. Yesterday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed the war in Gaza was the “opposite of a genocide” as protests erupted outside the UN.Across town at the glass-encased Javits Center, the mood was almost too serene. A swarm of museum curators, art advisors, and members of New York’s top tax brackets browsed the booths of the city’s premier art fair on Thursday. The Armory Show, which runs through Sunday, opened the previous day to an even more exclusive tier of VIPs, who returned to splurge on what they coveted. A smattering of celebrities including Jodie Foster, David Alan Grier, Piper Perabo, Paul Rudd, and Karl-Anthony Towns made the trek too, according to a fair spokesman.If collectors had any concerns about the wars or inflation, they did not share them.“They don’t care,” Michael Borghi, a dealer with Hollis Taggart, told Hyperallergic while gripping an abstract Stuart Davis painting he sold for more than $100,000. “They’re really rich individuals, they don’t care.” A view of the Armory Show's Platform section (photo Valentina Di Liscia/Hyperallergic)Sales on the first day of the fair appeared fairly steady. Michael Rosenfeld Gallery sold a Joan Mitchell painting for more than $2 million to a private collection, as well as collages by Louise Nevelson and Hannelore Baron, an Armory spokesman said. Over at Edwynn Houk Gallery, a László Moholy-Nagy gelatin silver print sold for $320,000. Gazelli Art House found a home for a Lilly Fenichel canvas with a European museum for $200,000, while Norr Cohan (formerly James Cohan Gallery) sold Yinka Shonibare’s “The Landscape Project (Cotton Plantation)” for more than $180,000, Nara Roesler sold Sheila Hicks’s “The soft side of my nature” (2025) for $260,000, and 303 Gallery placed two Rob Pruitt paintings for $155,000 each and a Doug Aitken lightbox for $150,000. Galerie Maximillian sold Rashid Johnson’s “Untitled (Large Mosaic)” (2025) for about $175,000 in the first hour of the fair, the Armory announced late Thursday evening. (Of course, it’s impossible to know whether these sales actually happened at the fair itself or via a PDF circulated months earlier.)

title: Arthur Jafa, King of Pop
description:
Art Review
                His eclectic references and intuitive grasp of memes and virality set him apart as an artist taking a
body:
Art Review
                His eclectic references and intuitive grasp of memes and virality set him apart as an artist taking assemblage and collage to new heights. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Installation view of Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony at the New Museum in Manhattan (photo Hakim Bishara/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Arthur Jafa’s survey I Am Tony at the New Museum in New York is full of the artist’s characteristic gallows humor that ironizes even the most morbid images and brings to the surface the solemnity of low culture. Occupying two levels of the Lower Manhattan institution, the exhibition is densely packed with work that ventures beyond the video art that has made Jafa one of America’s most important living artists. The largest exhibition of his work to date, its ambitions — which it achieves with mixed results — seem to be to engage in the same themes Jafa has continually mined, this time in even more idiosyncratic and brash ways. These include the history of Black music, religion and secularity, American cinema, political violence, popular culture, and the Internet. Arthur Jafa, "Allegiance" (1899, printed 2017), wallpaper (photo Stephanie Wambugu/Hyperallergic)One floor opens onto the aptly titled “Allegiance” (2026), a wall-to-wall black-and-white image of a crowd of 19th-century Black schoolchildren performing what looks like a “Sieg Heil,” while in the left quadrant, there is a boyish flag-bearer. The stars and stripes confirm that, despite initial appearances, this is a blown-up piece of Americana: a vernacular photograph of a once neutral, outmoded ritual. It has a grainy, spectral quality, and the way its young, somber subjects cluster in the frame produces a melancholic effect. The wall text explains that this gesture was once a customary and patriotic way of honoring the flag, but it is what that same salute came to mean in a 20th-century European context that gives this piece its power, which it derives through shock, juxtaposition, and new connotations that become apparent out of context. Installation view of Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony at the New Museum (photo Rebecca Schiffman/Hyperallergic)Another wallpaper, “Rwanda, 1999” (2026), is of a photo taken by Jafa at the Murambi Genocide Memorial in Rwanda, five years after the atrocity it observes took place. The bloodied garments of the mass killing’s victims are strewn across the entire museum wall. It’s impossible to view this without thinking of the genocide in Gaza, and one imagines its evocation was intentional on Jafa’s part, though the wall text does not explicitly mention Palestine.

title: Spring Break Art Show Tackles Life's Crushing Burdens
description:
Feature
                Fair participants touch on politics and current events through their own lens and invite others to do th
body:
Feature
                Fair participants touch on politics and current events through their own lens and invite others to do the same.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            From the artist's ongoing Peso Pesado series, Jesus Benavente's piñata sculptures capture the contemporary quality of life. (all photos Rhea Nayyar/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            The Spring Break Art Show returns to New York to do what it does best: host a labyrinthine art fair in a venue that was very evidently another business's heavily outfitted headquarters before being vacated. This time, visitors land up in the north side of Hell's Kitchen, weaving through the old CBS News offices where 60 Minutes, CBS Sports, and Inside Edition were hosted until earlier this year. While fixtures of the news outlet's branding and functions are still found throughout the 9th floor of 555 West 57th Street, Spring Break's participants continue to touch on politics and current events through their own lens and invite others to do the same. So much so that Everything Is Political, the independent media project launched by the climate justice nonprofit Slow Factory, has actually taken over one of the old CBS recording studios to create The People's Newsroom, where visitors are encouraged to go on the record and broadcast their own news, political takes, and other pressing matters.Slow Factory, The People’s Newsroom (2026)Though Slow Factory asks all of us to lay our thoughts out in the open, Spring Break's theme this year is “Hide 'n Seek” — an apt designation for the circuitous floor plan rife with dead-ends, hidden nooks, and other unusual places for artwork to nestle. “This is actually the perfect venue for the theme,” Andrew Gori, who co-founded Spring Break with Ambre Kelly, told Hyperallergic during a chance encounter on Thursday, September 24. “We had the chance to have the fair in TriBeCa again, but this felt better suited.”Luke Ivy Price, “Miss Wilma Cleans the Dryers” (2026) Curated by Ryan Bock, artist Luke Ivy Price's work focuses on unseen, quotidian, and maintenance labor that's essential to a functioning society, yet wholly under-appreciated, if not denigrated. Equally playful and provocative, “Hide 'n Seek” brought in conversations about labor and equity, intimacy and privacy, intentionally obfuscated histories and their domino-effect impact, and, as one would imagine, the politics of the body.
